raw_response:
I am 60 years old this year, and I have never been to school. I cannot read or write, but I know my land. My husband and I have two mouths to feed and 5.5 mu of land. We have been growing stevia for about eight years now, ever since Old Wang from the eastern part of the village said there was a buyer coming around every autumn offering cash for dried leaves. Before that we grew wheat and corn like everyone else, but the stevia pays a little better and we are too old now for the heavy harvest of grain.

I do not know kilograms and those fancy numbers. I think in bags and jin. This spring, like every spring, I will hire the young man with the small tractor to come rotary-till my field after the wheat stubble is cleared. I pay him about fifty yuan per mu. Then in late April, when the soil is warm and the apricot trees are blooming, I will buy my seedlings from the nursery in town. It costs me about one hundred fifty yuan per mu for the seedlings. I plant them by hand, me and my husband, bending down row by row. It takes us three hard days, and my back aches for a week after.

For fertilizer, I put down base fertilizer when I plant. I use one big bag of compound fertilizer per mu — about eighty jin — the kind with the three numbers on it that the shopkeeper gives me. That is what I have always done. After the first cut in late July, when the plants grow back, I topdress with half a bag of urea per mu, about thirty jin. If I do not put this down, the second cut is thin and yellow, and I learned that the hard way three years ago when I tried to save money.

I irrigate four times from my well. Once right after planting to help the seedlings settle, once in June when the weather gets hot, once after the first cut, and once more in August if the autumn drought comes. Pumping costs electricity money, and every time I turn on the pump my heart hurts a little watching the meter spin, but stevia cannot take dry spells. If the leaves turn small and bitter, the buyer pays less.

For pests, I spray when I see them. Usually once for weeds with herbicide after planting, and once or twice for insects in the summer when the green worms show up. The shop man tells me what to buy. Last year I spent about seventy yuan per mu on chemicals, and I expect the same this year.

I cut twice. First cut is in late July when the plants are about this tall — I use my hand sickle. The second cut is in mid-September before the frost comes. My husband and I do most of the cutting and drying, but we hire two women from the village for a few days each cut. We are not fast anymore, and the leaves must be cut before they flower or they turn bitter. We pay them one hundred yuan per day, and they get lunch. We dry the leaves on the concrete yard in front of the house, turning them every day. The buyer comes in a truck in late September and weighs everything.

I expect about one hundred fifty jin of dry leaves per mu if the weather is normal. Last year was a bit dry and I only got one hundred thirty, but two years ago was good and I got one hundred seventy. I would rather not hope too high.
